title: Moses Mendelssohn
hookLine: a Berlin philosopher who translated the Torah into German

cards: The challenge is printed on the first pages of a book, where anyone can read it.

A Swiss pastor named Johann Caspar Lavater has dedicated the book to a Jewish philosopher in Berlin, and challenges him in public: either show what is wrong with Christianity, or do what reason demands and be baptized.
Readers are watching. The philosopher is admired in the salons, praised by Christian friends, read in German. Now he must choose between attacking his neighbors' faith and leaving his own.

teach.h: A THIRD WAY: FIRM, AND AT PEACE.
teach.b: Mendelssohn took a third way. He wrote back, publicly, that he remained firm in his own faith and had no wish to go to war against anyone else's.
Judaism, he explained, does not go out looking for converts, and he did not want to spend his life in religious dispute. He would keep his faith and keep his friends.
That answer is Mendelssohn in miniature: a man living in two worlds and refusing to give either up.

teach.h: AN OBSERVANT JEW, A GERMAN PHILOSOPHER.
teach.b: He was an observant Jew who kept the commandments, and a German philosopher who wrote in elegant German about God, the soul and beauty. Then he brought those two worlds into one room.

teach.h: THE TORAH IN GERMAN, IN HEBREW LETTERS.
teach.b: He translated the Torah into German and had it printed in Hebrew letters, alongside the Hebrew text and a Hebrew commentary. A young Jew who read Hebrew could open the Torah and, line by line, learn a careful German too.
There's an old rabbinic way of thinking about that kind of bridge.

teach.h: JAPHETH IN THE TENTS OF SHEM.
teach.b: In Genesis, Noah blesses Shem and Japheth: "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem."
The Talmud, in tractate Megillah, reads that verse as permission to write the Torah in Greek, letting the beauty of Japheth live inside the tents of Shem.
Mendelssohn's translation made a similar wager: that a new language could live inside the Torah's tent without knocking it down. Not everyone agreed.
Some rabbis worried it would lead young people toward German and away from Torah. Others welcomed it. Both reactions are part of his story.

how: Mendelssohn's German translation of the Torah, with its Hebrew commentary known as the Biur, is studied by historians as a turning point, and his life is often discussed in Jewish schools as a model and a question about living in two cultures.

games.q: you're Moses Mendelssohn. a pastor publicly demands that you refute Christianity or be baptized. what do you answer?
o: write a fierce attack on Christianity.
say you remain firm in your faith and have no wish to fight anyone else's.
games.why: he declined both choices: firm in Judaism, unwilling to wage religious dispute, and keeping his Christian friends.

practice: Name two worlds you move between: work and home, the language of your parents and of your friends, a faith community and a secular office.
Picture each as a room, notice what you usually leave at the door, and ask whether one small thing from the first could come into the second without breaking either.
